en: Scatter our four kinds of livestock.
“She is a woman who ruined a people,
A wretch without propriety,” they will say,
And seize us on the road.
Making our wretched souls cry out,
They will sacrifice us today.
If this is a roaming enemy,
They will take their lingering vengeance on us.
They will not spare our little lives;
Mother, they will kill us for nothing.
Seen today, gone tomorrow—
Mother, was this world always such shit?
That dear bird, the wild duck,
Flies toward the steppe without turning back.
We have died wandering, ah,
Mother, the child born of my womb!’
Before she could close her mouth,
The earth was veiled in shimmering mist;
Ismayil, with seventy strongmen,
Drew near and reached them.
His own sister Kanykei,
Her bloody face torn,
Her black hair loose
Upon her great dark head—
When champion Ismayil saw his sister,
His golden-bladed battle-axe
He seized and strode forward,
Driving it against his own flank:
‘You who gave your hand to seven saints,
For whom seven holy ones opened the road,
My orphaned brother-in-law, if only you had not died!
Or else, toward Bukhara,
Turning and wandering like this,
My sister, my charger, if only you had not come!
You who gave your hand to six saints,
My lion brother-in-law, if only you had not died!
After his death, wandering to Bukhara,
My sister, my good fortune, if only you had not come!
Morning star of this world,
My charger brother-in-law, if only you had not died!
Turning your steps toward Bukhara,
Household of my charger,
If only you had not come wandering to Bukhara!
Of a vast curving mountain, the blue-necked
Ridge—like that were you, my khanly brother-in-law!
Never recoiling from stone,
Sharpened from steel,
Like iron were you, my khanly brother-in-law!
Youngest of six lions,
God's beloved mortal,
My magnanimous brother-in-law, if only you had not died!
Fleeing with your child upon your back,
Sister, if only you had not come wandering to Bukhara!’
As Ismayil raised his voice,
Shouting, ‘My brother-in-law!’
When he extended his spear,
The strongmen behind him,
When they too saw Ismayil,
Wailed, ‘Our brother-in-law!’
They too went about shouting.
Then your mourning sister Kanykei said:
‘The hillside horses have mottled heads;
When your noble brother-in-law passed away,
The male child left behind was still young.
Ninety thousand horses in the mountains,
Noble steeds and racers without sense—
I lost all my gathered wealth;
Oh, brother, there is no master to tend it!
The great dogs gathered
And attacked my migrating camp at Ken-Kol.
Cursed be my womanhood!
From those stately dogs
I left without taking vengeance.
Upon this great dark head of mine,
I lost your brother-in-law,
Brother, at only thirty-two.
The six scoundrels went mad;
Their thoughts turned elsewhere.
Sons of the same father as the bloodthirsty hero,
The six scoundrels were the younger wife's sons.
When your fortunate brother-in-law died,
When this wretched head knew plunder,
They wore me down;
When I pleaded, they would not hear.
The six scoundrels humiliated me
And openly used their force.
They plundered my Sarts in Talas;
Cursed be my womanhood!
I left without settling my grievance against those dogs.
Your khanly brother-in-law gathered silver;
The six scoundrels enjoyed its benefits;
I, your sister, bore the grief.
Your brother-in-law gathered gold;
The six scoundrels enjoyed its worth;
Your sister bore the torment.
When they robbed my fine cloth,
When the six scoundrels brought evil upon me,
When they found their chance against me,
When they struck my breast open,
When the dogs crushed me from above,
When they scattered the four kinds of livestock,
Saying, “She camps in unsuitable places,”
For a woman whose husband has died,
Her own family is close, I thought.
My wealth was worth less than a penny;
I scattered it and came, little brother.
Finding no one to rely on, to you,
Taking refuge because you were khan,
I fled, little brother.
Fleeing Talas, wandering on foot,
I came shooting and eating corncrakes.
If I struggled with the dogs,
I would be worn out, I thought, and came.
My gold was worth less than charcoal;
Grown fat, the six scoundrels raided my camp.
My silver was worth less than charcoal;
Grown fat, the six scoundrels acted from jealousy.
My silk was worth less than felt;
When my sovereign passed away,
He said, “I shall be an equal kinsman.”
The drops flowing from my eyes—
A mark upon my fleshy buttocks
Was left by the slave Abyke's whip.
I hid myself from Talas,
Suffering much plunder and humiliation;
Because I was exhausted,
I brought the orphan fleeing this way!
I hid myself in Ken-Kol;
A day of sorrow fell upon my head,
Semetey, left by the bloodthirsty hero,
I brought him fleeing this way!
That dear bird, the quail,
Flies apart toward the steppe.
Parted from all, I truly suffered humiliation
For this child your brother-in-law left.
Calling him the pennon fixed to a spear,
Without shame I hid him in my bosom,
Calling him the gift left by the magnanimous one.
Calling him the hoof left by the winged steed,
Unable to stay, I came wandering.
Calling him the chick left by the falcon,
Calling him the pennon fixed to a spear,
I hid my precious one in my bosom
And came wandering with a purpose.
Calling him the gift left by the magnanimous one,
Calling him a newly planted plane tree,
This poor head suffered torment.
Was he not left by my khan,
This dark-browed hawk?
This wretched soul bore sorrow.
How could I remain in Ken-Kol?
If those great dogs kept raving,
They would torment my only child.
As that dear bird, the wild duck, flies,
I came seeking the steppe.
Semetey, born of my womb,
My only hero child, born after long yearning—
I came for my child!
Hear my words, Ismayil:
The pennon fixed to the spear,
The gift left by the magnanimous one,
I carried away from Ken-Kol
And brought him to you.
May I perish if I call it my own land!
This dear child left by happiness,
Ismayil, may I perish if I call him mine!
Hang an amulet upon his neck;
I give him to you wholly.
Ismayil, raise your orphan!
Do not let the swan be eaten by a hawk;
This only child born in my misery,
Let no one call him another man's son!
Do not let the goose be eaten by a hawk;
This dear child I rely upon,
Accept him, I shall give him to you.
My dear little brother,
Let no one call him another man's son!
The reason I give him to you:
Among the Chinese on the ridges,
There is much vengeance against us.
When my noble lord was alive,
The Six Cities, the khan of Kokand,
Down as far as Margilan,
Broad Andijan, Samarkand—
He caused them grief and humiliation.
Beating it out of their people,
Six thousand ingots, a thousand otter pelts,
Every month beating their people,
Every month he took tribute.
Unable to bear his levies,
Every nation was left weeping.
If a man of Kokand caught us,
His eyes held hidden malice;
If those people had the strength,
They would strike me down.
Crookedness was in their words,
Malice was in their eyes.
If they found their chance,
They would smash me to pieces.
In hostile places they have vengeance;
Where grudges were made, grudges remain.
“They will humiliate us”—
I, your sister Kanykei, have that fear.
Your brother-in-law who has passed away,
I met him at fourteen;
At first I remained childless,
By your brother-in-law I bore
This orphan here,
At thirty-two years of age.
Praying to God for an only child,
I opened my treasury,
Hoping their blessings might reach me.
My vast treasury of gold,
To mendicants, the poor, and dervishes,
To those in want, I scattered it.
Spending my gold,
I poured it out, leaving none.
Tormenting my soul greatly,
Exhausting my strength greatly,
I prayed for my orphan.
A host of saints joined together;
This child was granted through repentance.
All the saints joined together;
This child was granted through blessing.
Khan Koshoi of the Katagan,
My dear father,
Whose blessing enriched the people,
Who brought light to those he favored,
The dear land of Seven Rivers,
He made it a homeland with his skill.
The Kyrgyz of Seven Rivers,
He contrived to make them one people.
A saint protected by Shay,
An old man whose words were healing,
He gave his hand to seventy saints;
Seven holy ones opened his road.
At Kokotoi's memorial feast,
Before the many mighty men,
Prophet Koshoi joined them;
Semetey was conceived through his blessing.
This tender gray-mottled falcon of mine,
This Semetey here,
My gray goshawk, my morning star,
My renowned flowing spring,
My dear child left by my khan.
For him I braided my hair upward,
I gained him in my extremity.
I have many days still to see;
Whom have I besides him?
I opened my mouth and kissed him,
Opened my eyes and saw him!
The prince's child—
How would it be if I gave him willingly?
“He is left by my khanly brother-in-law,” you might say;
The prince's only child—
How would it be if you accepted him willingly?
